body.p: Indexescharacteristics of good Index evaluation One of the most important jobs an editor or author has to do in connection with an index is evaluate the index after it has been submitted by the indexer. However, this task can be complicated by the fact that editors and authors may have little training in how indexes are or should be constructed.

section.title: Adherence to House Style
section.p: House style The first thing to check is whether the index adheres to the house style. This includes conventions for capitalization, alphabetization, cross-reference style, and typography.

section.title: Audience Suitability
section.p: AudienceUsers Terminologyaudience-appropriate The terminology used in the index must be appropriate for the intended audience. A medical textbook might include the term “oncology” in the index, while a general health book would use the term “cancer.”

section.title: Treatment of Metatopic
section.p: Metatopic The metatopic is the overarching subject of the book. A common error in indexes is to create a heading for the metatopic with long strings of undifferentiated locators. The metatopic should either be omitted from the index or broken down into specific subheadings.

section.title: Subject Coverage
section.p: Subject coverage Exhaustivity Depth of indexingExhaustivity An index should cover the full range of subjects discussed in the text. Exhaustivity refers to the inclusion of all relevant material. However, exhaustivity must go hand-in-hand with discrimination—not every passing mention of a topic deserves an index entry.
Acronyms Composite concepts Acronyms should generally be cross-referenced to the spelled-out form. Composite concepts may need to be indexed under more than one heading to ensure access.

section.title: Differentiated Locators
section.p: Undifferentiated locatorsDifferentiation of locators Differentiation of locators Long strings of page numbers following a heading without subheadings are known as undifferentiated locators. They make it difficult for the reader to find the specific information they need. The solution is to break the heading into subheadings, a process called differentiation of locators.
